outcomes.label: Per-student school funding
outcomes.caveat: Other sources place Texas between 42nd and 47th depending on fiscal year and whether construction and pensions are counted. Per-student figures are also pushed around by enrolment growth and local property values, not only by state appropriations.

outcomes.label: Adults without health insurance
outcomes.comparison: roughly double the national rate of 11.3%
outcomes.sourceName: U.S. Census Bureau, via Cover Texas Now
outcomes.caveat: Driven heavily by Texas not expanding Medicaid, which is a decision of the legislature and governor — but also by the state’s share of agricultural and self-employed work, and by federal subsidy rules that Congress sets.

outcomes.label: Children without health insurance
outcomes.comparison: more than double the national rate of 6.0%; nearly a quarter of all uninsured children in the U.S.
outcomes.sourceName: Georgetown Center for Children and Families
outcomes.caveat: Rose from 10.9% in 2022, a 29% increase. Enrolment paperwork after the pandemic coverage unwinding accounts for part of the rise; eligibility rules set in Austin account for part.

outcomes.label: Infant deaths after the 2021 six-week ban
outcomes.value: infant deaths rose 12.9% in the following year
outcomes.comparison: against a 1.8% rise in the rest of the United States
outcomes.caveat: A single-state time-series comparison, not a randomised finding. The authors attribute much of the rise to congenital anomalies diagnosed too late to act on under the ban. This concerns the 2021 law (SB 8 of the 87th), not any bill on this quiz.

outcomes.label: What households pay for electricity
outcomes.comparison: from 11.50¢ in 2020; delivered rates are running 14–19¢ in 2026, and some monthly bills have reached $600–$800
outcomes.caveat: This increase largely predates the data centre build-out. Natural gas prices, transmission construction, population growth and extreme weather all move retail rates. Treat it as what has happened to bills, not as a data centre effect.

outcomes.label: What data centres are forecast to draw
outcomes.value: ≈78 GW of data-centre demand projected by 2030
outcomes.comparison: against an all-time grid peak of 85.5 GW for the whole of Texas (Aug 2023). ERCOT’s own 2024 forecast for the same year was 29.6 GW — it has since more than doubled.
outcomes.sourceName: ERCOT long-term load forecast, via Data Center Dynamics
outcomes.caveat: A forecast built from interconnection requests, not built capacity — developers request far more than they finish, and ERCOT has revised this number sharply upward twice. Who pays for the transmission it needs is the live question, and is what SB 6 and the 2026 PUC actions are about.

outcomes.label: Spending on Operation Lone Star
outcomes.comparison: border security spending went from $800 million in 2018–19 to $6.6 billion in 2024–25; proposed appropriations would take the running total to roughly $18 billion
outcomes.caveat: Deliberately marked neutral. It has funded roughly 45 miles of state-built barrier, over 100 miles of razor wire and busing more than 119,000 people to other cities. Whether that is money well spent is the argument, not a fact this page can settle. Abbott has asked the federal government to reimburse it.

outcomes.label: Voter turnout
outcomes.comparison: behind every state except Hawaii, Oklahoma, Arkansas and West Virginia
outcomes.sourceName: Ballotpedia turnout analysis; U.S. Census Bureau
outcomes.caveat: Rank depends on the denominator: measured against voting-age citizens rather than eligible voters, Census estimates put Texas 2nd lowest at 57.9%. Turnout also tracks how competitive a state is thought to be, not registration law alone.

outcomes.label: Incarceration rate
outcomes.comparison: counting prisons, jails, immigration detention and juvenile facilities; Mississippi is highest, Massachusetts lowest at 96 per 100,000 in prison
outcomes.caveat: Down 18% over the past decade, so the trend runs the other way from the level. Rates vary a lot by which facility types a source counts.

outcomes.label: Job growth
outcomes.value: 132,500 jobs added in 2025 — more than any other state
outcomes.comparison: real GDP grew 4.8% in 2024, above the national rate; at $2.9 trillion Texas would be the world’s 8th largest economy on its own
outcomes.sourceName: Dallas Fed; Bureau of Labor Statistics via Visual Capitalist
outcomes.caveat: First place is in absolute jobs, which partly reflects being the second most populous state. By growth RATE Missouri led 2025 at +1.7%. Job counts also say nothing about pay: Texas has no state minimum wage above the federal $7.25.

outcomes.label: Property tax burden
outcomes.value: 1.245% effective rate — a median bill of $4,108
outcomes.comparison: against a national average rate of 0.888% and a national median bill of $3,211 — and Texas homes are worth less on average ($313,200 vs $360,600)
outcomes.sourceName: ATTOM property tax analysis, via Fox 4
outcomes.caveat: This is the direct trade-off for having no state income tax: schools, cities and counties are funded from local property levies instead. Whether that is the better deal depends on your income and whether you own. Rates also vary widely by county.

outcomes.label: Renters spending too much on rent
outcomes.comparison: of 4.1 million renter households; 23.6% are severely burdened, paying over half their income in rent. Median rent rose 9.1% after inflation while median household income rose 3.1%, to $78,476.
outcomes.sourceName: U.S. Census / American Community Survey, via Texas Tribune
outcomes.caveat: The burden is concentrated: about 90% of renters earning under $30,000 are cost-burdened, against a far lower share of higher earners, so a statewide average understates how hard it lands at the bottom. Rents are also set by local markets and land supply, not by state law alone.

outcomes.label: How much housing is being built
outcomes.value: 74,350 new residential permits in 2025 — more than any state
outcomes.comparison: Houston ranked 1st and Dallas 2nd among all U.S. cities for new permits, with San Antonio 8th and Austin 9th
outcomes.sourceName: Census building permits, via Wealth Enhancement / Consumer Affairs
outcomes.caveat: Permit volume fell about 9% from the previous year. First place is an absolute count, which partly reflects size and population growth. Note the tension with the figure above: leading the country in construction has not stopped affordability worsening faster here than nationally.

outcomes.label: Texans without a broadband connection
outcomes.comparison: either because the infrastructure does not reach them or because they are not subscribed; four of the five least-connected cities in the country are in Texas
outcomes.sourceName: Texas Consumer Association; National Digital Inclusion Alliance
outcomes.caveat: The 9 million figure combines two different problems — no service available, and service available but unaffordable — which need different fixes. The least-connected-cities ranking is from a 2019 analysis and may have moved since.

outcomes.label: Data privacy enforcement
outcomes.comparison: the largest state privacy recovery against Google by any attorney general, plus $1.4 billion from Meta over facial-recognition data in 2024
outcomes.sourceName: Office of the Texas Attorney General
outcomes.caveat: Secured by Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is a candidate in one of the three races here. Settlement size is not the same as consumer benefit — how much reaches Texans, versus the state treasury and outside counsel, is a separate question this figure does not answer.

outcomes.label: Who pays for a lawyer when you cannot afford one
outcomes.value: the state covers about 13% of the cost
outcomes.comparison: counties pay the rest. In 2013 counties spent $189.7 million against the state’s $27.4 million — 14 cents from the state for every county dollar.
outcomes.sourceName: Texas Indigent Defense Commission; Legislative Budget Board
outcomes.caveat: Marked neutral because it describes who bears a cost, not a ranking — whether the state or the county should fund the right to counsel is the argument. Note the dating: the 13% share is FY2020 and the dollar comparison is 2013, so both may have moved. The 13% is state grants offsetting county spending, not a share of total system cost.

outcomes.label: Exonerations
outcomes.value: more than 470 since 1989 — most of any state
outcomes.comparison: 26 in 2024 alone, ahead of Illinois on 20. Texas has also exonerated 18 people from death row, second only to Florida.
outcomes.caveat: Reads two opposite ways and the number cannot tell you which: it may mean more wrongful convictions, or better machinery for catching them. Both are partly true here. 17 of the 26 exonerations in 2024 trace to misconduct by a single Houston narcotics officer. Texas has also executed more people than any state since 1976.

outcomes.label: Firearm death rate
outcomes.comparison: against 28.0 in Mississippi (highest) and 3.7 in Hawaii (lowest)
outcomes.sourceName: Violence Policy Center, from CDC data
outcomes.caveat: Texas has the highest raw count of firearm deaths of any state, which mostly reflects being the second most populous. Per capita it sits in the middle of the states.

incumbents.name: Greg Abbott
acts: Signed or vetoed every bill that reached his desk in that time.
Vetoed 279 bills across those six regular sessions, 28 of them in the 89th.
Vetoed SB 3, the THC ban, which was the Lieutenant Governor’s third-ranked priority bill.
In 2026 directed the PUC and ERCOT to act on how data-centre costs are allocated, and froze new data-centre projects pending a state audit.

incumbents.name: Ken Paxton
acts: Set up a privacy enforcement team in 2024 and recovered $1.375 billion from Google and $1.4 billion from Meta over Texans’ data.
Has no roll-call record overlapping the three House candidates: his last legislative vote was in 2015, before any of them took office.
Was impeached by the Texas House in 2023 and acquitted by the Senate.

incumbents.name: Dan Patrick
acts: Presides over the Senate, assigns bills to committees and controls the calendar.
Published a numbered priority-bill list each session — 25 bills in the 89th.
Does not cast a vote except to break a tie, so he has no roll-call record to score.

causalNote: These numbers are where Texas stands, from the sources named. They are not proof that any one vote, bill or official caused them — rankings move on population growth, local property values, federal rules and the economy as well as state law. What is on the record is the outcome, the vote, and who held office. Draw your own line between them.

omissions.why: Published 2024 road-death figures for Texas conflict (1,997 vs 4,150) and could not be reconciled to a primary source.
No outcome measure exists here that is not itself a value judgement.

opponents.name: Dan Patrick
opponents.whyNoVotes: Presides over the Senate rather than voting in the House, so he casts no vote on these bills.
opponents.evidence: priority-bill designations — bills he publicly named as must-pass
opponents.oneSided: Every bill on that list is one he wanted passed, so it can show where he stood on a bill but never how often he would agree with you.

opponents.name: Greg Abbott
opponents.whyNoVotes: Has never served in a legislature, so he has no roll-call record at all.
opponents.evidence: what he did with each bill that reached him — signed it, vetoed it, or let it become law without signing
opponents.oneSided: Every bill that reaches a governor gets one of three answers, so unlike a priority list this can show both directions. It is still uneven: he signed 27 of the 32 that reached him, so a signature mostly means he did not object rather than that he pushed. The 4 he let become law without signing are recorded as taking no side, because that is what they are. 35 of these bills never reached his desk at all, and he appears on none of those.

opponents.name: Ken Paxton
opponents.whyNoVotes: His last legislative vote was in 2015, before any of the three took office — there is no session they share.
opponents.evidence: nothing that attaches to these bills
opponents.oneSided: Nothing on his record can be joined to a bill in this quiz, so he appears on no question.

comparatorRule: From each caucus: the most party-line member, the median member, and the member who most often broke ranks. The same rule on both sides, recomputed every build.
candidateProvenance: This page is about three specific races: Governor, Lieutenant Governor and U.S. Senate. All three Democratic candidates sit in the Texas House, which is the reason the comparison works at all — they voted on the same bills you are being asked about, so their records can be checked against yours vote for vote. Choosing those three races is an editorial decision, not a measurement, and the six other members below each question are picked by rule from both parties so the page is not left showing one side of the chamber.
plainLanguageNote: The short description under a bill is written by us, not copied from the record, and only the seven headline bills have one. Every other question shows the official caption on its own.

items.caption: Relating to information regarding perinatal palliative care; creating an administrative penalty.
items.plain: Requires the state to produce information about perinatal palliative care, and requires a doctor to give it to a pregnant woman when an unborn child is diagnosed with a life-limiting condition.

items.caption: Relating to the duty of the attorney general to prosecute criminal offenses prescribed by the election laws of this state.
items.plain: Lets the attorney general prosecute election-law crimes when the local prosecutor has not acted within six months of receiving a police report.

items.caption: Relating to certain prohibited transactions and logistical support between a governmental entity and an abortion assistance entity or abortion provider for the procurement of an abortion or related services.
items.plain: Bars cities and counties from spending public money or giving logistical support to abortion providers, or to groups that help people obtain an abortion.

items.caption: Relating to the Texas presidential library promotion program and funding for the program.
items.plain: Creates a state program and fund to promote the presidential libraries in Texas as historical and tourist attractions.

items.caption: Relating to the licensing and regulation of music therapists; requiring an occupational license; authorizing fees.
items.plain: Requires music therapists to hold a state licence before they can practise, and allows the state to charge fees for it.

items.caption: Relating to the Texas moving image industry incentive program and the establishment and funding of the Texas moving image industry incentive fund.
items.plain: Creates a state fund that pays incentives to film and television productions, and lets the state refuse a grant over content it judges indecent or unflattering to Texas.

items.caption: Relating to the eligibility of the South by Southwest Conference and Festivals for funding under the Major Events Reimbursement Program.
items.plain: Makes South by Southwest eligible for state event-reimbursement money, and exempts it from having to show it considered holding the festival outside Texas.

items.caption: Relating to the eligibility of certain events for funding under the major events reimbursement program.
items.plain: Makes an FIA World Endurance Championship car race eligible for state event-reimbursement money.

items.caption: Relating to the eligibility of the American Performance Horseman and the American Rodeo for funding under the major events reimbursement program.
items.plain: Makes the American Performance Horseman and the American Rodeo eligible for state event-reimbursement money.

items.caption: Relating to the authority of a county to dispose of surplus and salvage property to a civic or charitable organization.
items.plain: Lets a county donate surplus property to a civic or charitable group without first having to show that selling it at auction would fail.

items.caption: Relating to affidavits concerning cost and necessity of services in civil actions.
items.plain: For medical bills of $50,000 or less, removes the need for a sworn affidavit to prove the charges were reasonable and the care was necessary.

items.caption: Relating to procedures for changes to a zoning regulation or district boundary.
items.plain: Makes it harder for neighbours to force a supermajority vote on a rezoning: an adjoining-owner protest now needs 60% of that land, and the council can then approve the change by simple majority.

items.caption: Relating to the award of diligent participation credit to defendants confined in a state jail felony facility.
items.plain: Makes time credit automatic, rather than up to the judge, for state jail inmates who take part in an education, treatment or work programme.

items.caption: Relating to civil asset forfeiture of digital currency or other similar property.
items.plain: Lets the state seize cryptocurrency through civil forfeiture, by adding digital currency to the property that can be taken as suspected proceeds of a crime.

items.caption: Relating to the authority of certain peace officers to arrest a person without a warrant while outside the officer's jurisdiction.
items.plain: Lets police officers employed by water districts arrest people without a warrant outside their own jurisdiction, for offences committed in front of them.

items.caption: Relating to the establishment by the Texas Workforce Commission of a pilot program to train workers for careers in energy-efficient technologies.
items.plain: Creates a pilot programme in Dallas-Fort Worth in which the state, community colleges and employers train workers for jobs in energy-efficient technology.

items.caption: Relating to a severance payment to a superintendent of a school district.
items.plain: Caps what a school district can pay a departing superintendent at six months of salary and benefits, and requires the payment to be reported.

items.caption: Relating to the bilingual education allotment under the public school finance system.
items.plain: Requires school districts excused from running a bilingual programme to report which alternative language methods they use, so those methods count towards bilingual education funding.

items.caption: Relating to an application for an early voting ballot by mail.
items.plain: Makes one mail-in ballot application cover both the election and any runoff, unless the voter asks not to be sent the runoff ballot.

items.caption: Relating to requiring notice to the attorney general in an action under the Election Code seeking a temporary restraining order.
items.plain: Requires a court to notify the attorney general before it hears a request for a temporary restraining order in an election case.

items.caption: Relating to the regulation of campaign treasurer appointments and related matters and the content of and posting of information contained in a campaign treasurer appointment; providing a civil penalty.
items.plain: Sets who may serve as a campaign treasurer: at least 18, a Texas resident, not already treasurer for someone else, and not convicted of certain election offences.

items.caption: Relating to the establishment of the office of food system security and resiliency in the Department of Agriculture and the management of the Texas food system security and resiliency planning council.
items.plain: Creates an office inside the Department of Agriculture responsible for keeping the state's food supply secure and free of disruption.

items.caption: Proposing a constitutional amendment to authorize the use of money from the Texas energy fund for energy efficiency projects conducted to benefit retail electric customers.
items.plain: Asks voters to change the constitution so money from the Texas energy fund can pay for energy-efficiency projects that benefit electricity customers.

items.caption: Relating to the calculation of the voter-approval tax rate for certain municipalities that receive municipal hotel occupancy tax revenue and other money from a local park board of trustees.
items.plain: Creates a separate formula for the tax rate a coastal city can set without voter approval, based on hotel tax revenue the city has misspent.

items.caption: Relating to the age of criminal responsibility and to certain substantive and procedural matters related to that age.
items.plain: Raises the age at which someone is tried as an adult from 17 to 18, so 17-year-olds go through the juvenile system instead.

items.caption: Relating to parole guidelines and procedures for inmates convicted of an offense committed when younger than 18 years of age.
items.plain: Requires the parole board to write separate guidelines for people convicted of crimes they committed before turning 18, weighing rehabilitation and education.

items.caption: Relating to the required number of minutes of instructional time to be provided by a juvenile justice alternative education program.
items.plain: Changes what juvenile justice alternative schools must provide from seven hours a day for 180 days to 43,200 minutes of instruction a year.

items.caption: Relating to prohibiting the recognition, service, and enforcement of extreme risk protective orders; creating a criminal offense.
items.plain: Bars Texas courts and agencies from recognising or enforcing red-flag orders that remove firearms from someone judged a risk, and makes doing so a crime.

items.caption: Relating to municipal and county firearm buyback programs.
items.plain: Bans cities and counties from running or taking part in gun buyback programmes.

items.caption: Relating to the carrying of handguns by tactical medical professionals while on duty providing support to tactical units of law enforcement agencies.
items.plain: Lets paramedics attached to police tactical units carry a handgun on duty, and shields their agency from liability if it is fired.

items.caption: Relating to a study on the coverage of certain infants under Medicaid.
items.plain: Orders a state study of whether newborns whose mothers were on Medicaid are getting the coverage federal rules require.

items.caption: Relating to conducting an assessment of language accessibility with respect to certain health and human services programs and 2-1-1 services provided by the Texas Information and Referral Network.

statements.text: I was excused to attend a meeting of the Committee on Public Education. I would have voted yes.

items.plain: Requires the state to hire a language access coordinator and find where people who do not speak English cannot reach health and social services or 2-1-1.

items.caption: Relating to the establishment of the governor's task force on the governance of early childhood education and care.
items.plain: Creates a governor's task force to examine how early childhood education and childcare are run in Texas.

items.caption: Relating to the issuance of a certified birth record to a homeless individual.
items.plain: Requires the state to give a homeless person a free certified copy of their birth certificate when they ask for one.

items.caption: Relating to the implementation of a statewide homeless data sharing network to share real-time data on homelessness.
items.plain: Requires the state housing agency to build a statewide network for sharing real-time data on homelessness.

items.caption: Relating to size and density requirements for residential lots in certain municipalities; authorizing a fee.
items.plain: Stops larger cities from requiring a new house lot to be bigger than 3,000 square feet, wider than 30 feet or deeper than 75 feet, on newly platted land of five acres or more.

items.caption: Relating to the purchase or acquisition of an interest in real property by certain aliens or foreign entities; creating a criminal offense; providing a civil penalty.
items.plain: Bars people and companies tied to certain foreign governments, China among them, from buying land or property in Texas, and makes doing so a crime.

items.caption: Relating to the establishment of the Texas Commission on Border Security and Illegal Immigration.
items.plain: Creates an 11-member advisory commission of state officials and legislators to study border security and illegal immigration.

items.caption: Relating to creating the criminal offenses of transnational repression and unauthorized enforcement of foreign law and to a study and law enforcement training regarding transnational repression.

statements.text: I was shown voting no. I intended to vote yes.

items.plain: Makes it a crime to act for a foreign government in threatening, assaulting or stalking someone in Texas, or to enforce another country's laws here.

items.caption: Relating to county jailer training on interacting with veterans in the criminal justice system.
items.plain: Requires the state to create training for county jailers on dealing with veterans in custody.

items.caption: Relating to the administration, powers, and duties of the Texas Space Commission and Texas Aerospace Research and Space Economy Consortium, to other governmental entities regarding aerospace, aviation, and space exploration initiatives and activities, and to the abolishment of the spaceport trust fund.
items.plain: Reorganises the state's space agencies, widens the aerospace office's remit from space to aviation as well, and abolishes the spaceport trust fund.

items.caption: Relating to waiver programs for certain veterans provided by toll project entities.
items.plain: Requires toll road operators to let certain veterans drive free, rather than leaving it optional or allowing a discount instead.

items.caption: Relating to the regulation of elevator mechanics, elevator apprentices, and contractors; requiring an occupational registration.
items.plain: Requires elevator mechanics, apprentices and contractors to register with the state before working on elevators.

items.caption: Relating to the effect of a disaster and associated costs on the calculation of certain tax rates and the procedure for adoption of a tax rate by a taxing unit.
items.plain: Lets a local government in a declared disaster area use a different formula for the tax rate it can set without voter approval, based on its disaster relief costs.

items.caption: Relating to measures for ensuring public school safety, including the commissioning of peace officers by the Texas Education Agency, the composition of the board of directors of the Texas School Safety Center, and public school safety and security requirements and resources.
items.plain: Lets the Texas Education Agency commission its own police officers, and changes school safety rules and who sits on the state's School Safety Center board.

items.caption: Relating to measures to assist students enrolled at public institutions of higher education who are homeless or who are or were in foster care.
items.plain: Extends the help colleges must give students who were in foster care — including a named staff liaison — to students who are homeless.

items.caption: Relating to general definitions for and collection of governmental information regarding biological sex.
items.plain: Writes definitions of male and female into state law and requires government records that collect sex to use them.

items.caption: Relating to risk mitigation planning and associated liability for providers of electric service; providing an administrative penalty.
items.plain: Lets electric utilities self-insure against wildfire losses and requires them to file wildfire risk plans, with a penalty for failing to.

items.caption: Relating to the residential and commercial building codes of municipalities.
items.plain: Updates the building codes Texas cities must use for homes and commercial buildings from the 2012 editions to the 2018 editions.

items.caption: Relating to the authority of certain persons to obtain third-party review of plats and property development plans, permits, and similar documents, and the inspection of an improvement related to such a document.
items.plain: Lets an applicant have a licensed engineer review or inspect development documents, instead of waiting for the local government to do it.

items.caption: Relating to county regulation related to infrastructure planning for subdivisions and county authority to regulate building and set-back lines.
items.plain: Stops counties from limiting how many homes can be built per acre outside city limits, including through minimum lot sizes, lot widths or setbacks.

items.caption: Relating to the approval of land use assumptions, capital improvement plans, and impact fees.
items.plain: Requires a local government to publish its growth assumptions and capital plans 60 days before the hearing on new impact fees, rather than on the day of notice.

items.caption: Relating to the authority of certain counties to impose a hotel occupancy tax.
items.plain: Lets the county where the Guadalupe River rises charge its own hotel tax, except at hotels a city already taxes.

items.caption: Relating to the authority of certain counties to impose a hotel occupancy tax.
items.plain: Lets the county where the Llano and James rivers meet charge its own hotel tax, except at hotels a city already taxes.

items.caption: Relating to the periodic reappraisal of property by, and the prohibition on posting on the Internet certain information held by, an appraisal district.
items.plain: Lets appraisal districts put more property images online, including street-level exterior photos and aerial shots showing more than one building.

items.caption: Relating to a health care facility grant program supporting the use of artificial intelligence technology in scanning medical images for cancer detection.
items.plain: Creates a state grant programme to help Texas hospitals and clinics use artificial intelligence to scan medical images for cancer.

items.caption: Relating to the definition of authorized peace officer for purposes of certain laws governing the installation and use of tracking equipment and access to certain communications.
items.plain: Adds state insurance investigators to the officers allowed to use tracking devices and to obtain access to certain communications.

items.caption: Relating to transportation planning by metropolitan planning organizations.
items.plain: Requires regional transport planners to take account of the travel needs of people who use state health, welfare and workforce services.

items.caption: Relating to automobile liability insurance requirements for transportation network company drivers.
items.plain: Rewrites the insurance a rideshare driver must carry, separating cover while they are logged on and waiting from cover while a passenger is in the car.

items.caption: Relating to towing fee studies and the amount of nonconsent towing fees in certain political subdivisions; authorizing an increase in existing fees; authorizing a fee.

statements.text: I was shown voting yes. I intended to vote no.

items.plain: Requires local governments that cap non-consent towing fees to review those fees at least every two years, and allows the caps to be raised.

items.label: School vouchers
items.why: The marquee fight of the session: public money for private school tuition. Lt. Gov. priority bill.
items.plain: Creates state-funded accounts that families can spend on private school tuition and other approved school costs. The money comes out of the state budget.
items.caption: Relating to the establishment of an education savings account program.

items.label: Immigration enforcement
items.why: Requires local law enforcement to assist federal deportation efforts. Lt. Gov. priority bill.
items.plain: Requires sheriffs to sign agreements letting their deputies carry out federal immigration enforcement, and creates state grants to pay for doing it.
items.caption: Relating to agreements between certain sheriffs and the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement to enforce federal immigration law and a grant program to cover the costs of implementing those agreements.

items.label: Ten Commandments in classrooms
items.why: Requires the Ten Commandments displayed in public schools. Lt. Gov. priority bill.
items.plain: Requires every public school classroom in Texas to display a copy of the Ten Commandments.
items.caption: Relating to the display of the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms.

items.label: THC ban
items.why: Lt. Gov. priority bill that the Governor then VETOED — a documented split between two Republican leaders on one bill.
items.plain: Bans hemp products containing THC — the ones sold in smoke shops and convenience stores — and adds licences, fees and criminal penalties for selling them.
items.caption: Relating to the regulation of products derived from hemp, including consumable hemp products and the hemp-derived cannabinoids contained in those products; requiring occupational licenses and permits; imposing fees; creating criminal offenses; authorizing an administrative penalty.

statements.text: my vote failed to register. I would have voted no.

items.label: Regulatory review ("Texas DOGE")
items.why: Creates a state office to review regulations. Lt. Gov. priority bill.
items.plain: Sets up a new state office to review the rules that agencies write, and tells judges to stop treating an agency’s own reading of the law as the correct one.
items.caption: Relating to reforming the procedure by which state agencies adopt rules and impose regulatory requirements and the deference given to the interpretation of laws and rules by state agencies in certain judicial proceedings.

items.label: Electric grid and large power users
items.why: Grid reliability rules for large loads such as data centres. Lt. Gov. priority bill.
items.plain: Sets the rules for how very large electricity users, such as data centres, connect to the Texas grid and how much of the cost of serving them they pay.
items.caption: Relating to the planning for, interconnection and operation of, and costs related to providing service for certain electrical loads and to the generation of electric power by a water supply or sewer service corporation.

items.label: Dementia research institute
items.why: Creates a state dementia research institute. Included deliberately as the least party-coded of the headline bills — without it the short set would be entirely party-line.
items.plain: Creates a state institute that funds dementia prevention and research.
items.caption: Relating to the creation of the Dementia Prevention and Research Institute of Texas.
